sources.title: L. V. Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, 3rd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 1979)
sources.locator: Ch. 4 §2.1 (printed pp. 114–118) and Ch. 4 §4, §§4.1–4.7 (printed pp. 137–148), both read in full; Ch. 4 §§1.1–1.5, 2.2–2.3, 3.1–3.4 and §5 are outside the claimed range

contents.name: §2.1 The Index of a Point with Respect to a Closed Curve
Lemma 1 (the integral of $dz/(z-a)$ over a closed piecewise differentiable curve is a multiple of $2\pi i$)
Exercise 1 to §2.1 (alternate proof by subdividing $\gamma$ into subarcs carrying a single-valued branch of $\arg(z-a)$, with the compactness argument)
Exercise 2 to §2.1 (defining $n(\gamma,a)$ for a merely continuous closed curve by subdivision, and checking the properties survive)
Property (i) (a curve inside a circle has index $0$ at every point outside it)
Property (ii) (the index is constant on each complementary region and zero on the unbounded one; the complement determines exactly one unbounded region)
the statement that the complement of a compact curve determines one and only one unbounded region
the reversal law $n(-\gamma,a)=-n(\gamma,a)$
Lemma 2 (if $z_1$ lies in the lower half plane, $z_2$ in the upper, the subarc $\gamma_1$ misses the negative axis and $\gamma_2$ misses the positive axis, then $n(\gamma,0)=1$)
contents.reason: A geometric recognition criterion for the value 1, whose proof cuts the curve at two half-line crossings and adds three auxiliary closed curves. Nothing on this page needs to recognise the index from a picture: every index computed here is computed from the integral or from chain additivity. Its actual use in the source is the half of the Jordan curve theorem in Exercise 3, which belongs with the planar topology of domains.

contents.name: Exercise 3 to §2.1 (the complement of a Jordan curve has at least two components, proved from winding numbers)
contents.reason: The Jordan curve theorem for a general continuous simple closed curve is planar topology, not complex integration; this page establishes no separation theorem and needs none. Its half-proof rests on Lemma 2, also declined here.

contents.name: §4.1 Chains and Cycles
the definition of $\int_\Gamma f\,dz$ over a chain, and the criterion that a chain is a cycle exactly when initial and end points cancel in pairs
the additive law $n(\gamma_1+\gamma_2,a)=n(\gamma_1,a)+n(\gamma_2,a)$ for cycles
§4.2 Simple Connectivity, and Definition 1 (a region is simply connected when its complement in the EXTENDED plane is connected)
contents.reason: This definition is taken in the extended plane, so it needs the point at infinity and the topology of the Riemann sphere, neither of which is available from this page’s declared prerequisites. The design for this track fixes the homological adjective here and puts the meeting of the two notions on the later equivalence page.

contents.name: Theorem 14 ($\Omega$ is simply connected in the extended-plane sense iff $n(\gamma,a)=0$ for every cycle in $\Omega$ and every $a\notin\Omega$)
contents.reason: This is exactly the bridge between the extended-plane definition and the homological one, so it cannot be stated before the extended plane exists in the reading order. Its proof also needs the square-net construction over a net of side less than the separation of two disjoint closed complementary pieces, which is the same construction declined for §4.5.

contents.name: §4.3 Homology, and Definition 2 (a cycle is homologous to zero in $\Omega$ when $n(\gamma,a)=0$ for all $a$ in the complement)
§4.4 The General Statement of Cauchy’s Theorem, Theorem 15
Corollary 1 (Cauchy’s theorem holds for every cycle in a simply connected region)
Corollary 2 (on a simply connected region a nonvanishing analytic $f$ has single-valued analytic branches of $\log f$ and $\sqrt[n]{f}$)
the remark that on a simply connected region every analytic function is a derivative

§4.5 Proof of Cauchy’s Theorem (the square-net proof due to Beardon: cover the plane by a net of side $\delta$, take the boundary cycle $\Gamma_\delta$ of the union of closed squares inside $\Omega$, and reverse the order of the iterated integral)
contents.reason: A genuinely different second proof of a theorem this page already proves is welcome, but this one turns on reversing the order of two contour integrals taken over rectifiable cycles. The library’s Fubini theorem is for the Riemann integral on a product of closed rectangles; supplying the interchange for Riemann–Stieltjes integrators against two bounded-variation parameters is a prerequisite of its own and is not built here. Recorded so the second proof can be commissioned deliberately rather than lost.

contents.name: §4.6 Locally Exact Differentials, Theorem 16 ($\int_\gamma p\,dx+q\,dy=0$ for every cycle homologous to zero, for every locally exact differential), with Artin’s proof
contents.reason: This is the statement for a closed real 1-form rather than for $f\,dz$, and it is strictly more general than the holomorphic case this page needs. Building it here would mean carrying the real-form machinery and Artin’s rectangle-lattice reduction alongside the complex development, for no item on this page. It belongs with the de Rham theory of plane open sets.

contents.name: §4.7 Multiply Connected Regions: finite connectivity, the cycles $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_{n-1}$ forming a homology basis, and the uniqueness of the basis representation
contents.reason: Constructing the basis cycles $\gamma_i$ with $n(\gamma_i,a)=1$ on the $i$th complementary component uses the same square-net construction as Theorem 14, declined above. The concrete case the design asks for, the annulus with one period, is built as a companion example without that construction.

contents.name: §4.7 modules of periodicity: the integral over any cycle is an integer combination of the periods, illustrated on the annulus $r_1<|z|<r_2$

contents.name: Lemma 3.4.1 (a jointly continuous integrand holomorphic in the parameter integrates over $[0,1]$ to a holomorphic function), with the Morera–Fubini proof and the Wirtinger proof
Corollary 3.4.2 (the same statement with the interval replaced by a chain)
Corollary 3.4.3 (the Cauchy transform of a continuous boundary function is holomorphic inside the disc)
Definition 3.4.4 (uniform convergence on compact subsets)
Theorem 3.4.5 (a compactly uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, with convergence of all derivatives)
§4.1.1 The logarithm: the principal branch $\operatorname{Log}$ as the primitive of $1/z$ on the slit plane normalised at $1$, and the identity $\operatorname{Log}z=\log|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}z$
the multivalued $\log z=\log|z|+i\arg z$, a branch of the logarithm on an open set, and following a branch along a path through overlapping discs
Definition 4.1.1 (the winding number $n(\Gamma;p)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)$ of a cycle about a point off it)
Proposition 4.1.2 (the winding number is an integer), proved by covering the path by finitely many discs missing $p$ and matching branches of $\log(z-p)$ in sequence

Proposition 4.1.3 (the winding number is constant on the topological components of the complement, and zero on the unbounded component), with the explicit continuity estimate $|n(\Gamma;p_0)-n(\Gamma;p)|\le \ell|p_0-p|/(\pi d^2)$
the assertion that a compact $\Gamma$ leaves exactly one unbounded complementary component
Exercise 4.1.7 (the path $p+re^{int}$ has winding number $n$ at every point of $\Delta_r(p)$)
Exercise 4.1.8 (the outer circle minus the inner circle has index $0$, $1$, $0$ across the three regions)

Definition 4.2.1 (a cycle is homologous to zero in $U$ when its index vanishes at every point of $\mathbb C\setminus U$), with the warning that this does not mean equal to zero and that it depends on $U$
Theorem 4.2.2 (Cauchy integral formula, homology version), with Dixon’s 1971 proof through the filled difference quotient $g(\zeta,z)$ and the glued entire function $h$
Exercise 4.2.1 (that $g(\zeta,z)$ is continuous on $U\times U$ and holomorphic in $z$ for each fixed $\zeta$)
the estimate $|h(z)|\le M\ell/d(z,\Gamma)$ on the unbounded component and the appeal to Liouville
Theorem 4.2.3 (Cauchy’s theorem, homology version), deduced by applying the formula to $\zeta\mapsto(\zeta-z)f(\zeta)$
Definition 4.2.4 (two cycles are homologous in $U$ when their indices agree off $U$)
Corollary 4.2.5 (holomorphic integrals agree on homologous cycles)
Definition 4.3.1 (a domain is simply connected, in the homology sense, when every cycle in it is homologous to zero)
Exercise 4.3.1(a) (every star-like domain is simply connected) and 4.3.1(b) ($\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ is not)
Theorem 4.3.2 (Cauchy’s theorem, simply connected version)
Theorem 4.3.3 (every holomorphic function on a simply connected domain has a primitive), by reducing to the star-like case on a disc
Corollary 4.3.4 (a nowhere-zero holomorphic function on a simply connected domain has a holomorphic logarithm), via a primitive of $f’/f$
Corollary 4.3.5 (and hence a holomorphic $k$th root for every $k$)

Proposition 4.3.6 (six equivalent characterisations: null-homologous cycles, primitives, logarithms, a primitive for $1/(z-p)$, vanishing holomorphic cycle integrals, vanishing kernel cycle integrals)
Proposition 4.3.7 (if $\mathbb C_\infty\setminus U$ is connected then $U$ is simply connected), and the remark that the extended plane is essential
contents.reason: The hypothesis is stated in the Riemann sphere, and the proof extends the index function continuously by the value $0$ at infinity. Neither the sphere nor its topology is reachable from this page’s declared prerequisites, and the source itself defers the converse to its Riemann-mapping chapter.

contents.name: the remark that the existence of square roots also belongs on the equivalence list, with the proof deferred to the Riemann mapping theorem
contents.reason: Adding the square-root clause to the equivalence theorem needs the direction that a domain carrying square roots is simply connected, which the source itself obtains only from the Riemann mapping theorem. The easy direction is already on this page as the holomorphic-roots corollary.

sources.title: M. Weber, Complex Analysis (Indiana University, 2026)
sources.locator: Ch. 4 §4.1 "Cauchy’s Theorem" (PDF pp. 55–62), read in full; §§4.2–4.4 are outside the claimed range

contents.name: §4.1 Cauchy’s Theorem: the framing question, for which closed paths in $U$ does every holomorphic function integrate to zero
Definition 4.1.1 (the winding number of a closed path about a point off it)
the angle sum $\angle(\gamma)=\sum_k\angle(\gamma(t_{k-1}),\gamma(t_k))$ over a partition whose subarcs lie in open half planes, and its independence of the partition
Lemma 4.1.2 ($\angle(\gamma)$ is an integral multiple of $2\pi$ for a closed curve)
Lemma 4.1.3 ($\angle(\gamma_t)$ is constant along a homotopy of closed curves avoiding the origin)
contents.reason: Homotopy invariance of the index is the homotopy half of the theory; this page fixes the homological adjective deliberately and develops no homotopy of curves, so the statement has no consumer here and its hypotheses would have to be imported wholesale.

contents.name: Proposition 4.1.4 ($\angle(\gamma,a)$ equals $n(\gamma,a)$), proved by covering $\gamma$ with overlapping discs and matching antiderivatives of $1/z$
Definition 4.1.5 (a chain is a formal finite integer combination of curves in $U$; a cycle is a chain of closed curves) and the extension of the integral and the winding number by linearity
the extension of the integral and of the winding number to chains by linearity
Definition 4.1.6 (null homologous in $U$; two chains homologous when their difference is a null homologous cycle)

Theorem 4.1.7 (Cauchy’s Integral Theorem: both $\int_\gamma f=0$ and the index-weighted integral formula), first proof through the continuous extension of $g(w,z)$ to the diagonal and the entire extension $h$
the diagonal continuity estimate $g(w,z)-g(z_0,z_0)=(w-z)^{-1}\int_z^w (f’(t)-f’(z_0))\,dt$

the second, lattice proof of Theorem 4.1.7: replace $\gamma$ by an $\varepsilon$-path on a square lattice, cancel enclosed squares, and observe that every edge is then used equally often in both directions
contents.reason: A second route to the same theorem, welcome in principle, but it rests on replacing a rectifiable cycle by a lattice path with the same integral for every holomorphic function and on a combinatorial edge-counting argument over the lattice. Both are substantial constructions with no other consumer on this page, and the first proof is already built here in full.

contents.name: Definition 4.1.8 (the residue of an isolated singularity as the coefficient $a_{-1}$ of the Laurent series)
contents.reason: The residue is defined from the Laurent expansion, which this page does not have and does not need; the global Cauchy theorem is what the Laurent development will later rest on, not the other way round.

contents.name: Corollary 4.1.9 (the Residue Theorem: $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\gamma f=\sum_{s\in S}n(\gamma,s)\operatorname{res}_s f$)
contents.reason: The residue theorem is the first consumer of this page’s index-weighted formula, and it needs residues, hence Laurent series. Building it here would invert the reading order the plan fixes.

canonical.name: the approximation of a rectifiable contour integral by tagged sums, with an oscillation-times-length bound
removability of a continuous singularity: continuous on an open set and holomorphic off one point implies holomorphic
a holomorphic logarithm is a primitive of the logarithmic derivative
a disc missing $p$ carries a holomorphic logarithm of $z-p$
existence and $2\pi i\mathbb Z$-uniqueness of a continuous logarithm along a contour
the exterior of a closed disc in the plane is path-connected
the index of a cycle is an integer, from the boundary-zero condition
the integral of a continuous derivative over a cycle vanishes
the index of a cycle is locally constant off its trace and vanishes far from it
the filled difference quotient is holomorphic in each variable separately
the Cauchy transform of a cycle is holomorphic off the trace
the higher-derivative form of the global Cauchy formula
the winding number is attached to the parametrised contour, not to its trace
a connected plane domain need not be homologically simply connected
a nonvanishing holomorphic function on a domain need not have a holomorphic logarithm
the winding number read as the circulation of the planar vortex field, the same fact as the closed-not-exact form on the punctured plane
the conventions governing chains, cycles and the homological adjective on this page

sources.title: J. Lebl, Tasty Bits of Several Complex Variables, v4.4
sources.locator: Ch. 1 §§1.1–1.6 (PDF pp. 13–46), read in full; Ch. 2 onward and the appendices are outside the claimed range

contents.name: §1.1 Onto several variables: $\mathbb C^n$, holomorphic and antiholomorphic coordinates, the Euclidean inner product and norm
Definition 1.1.1 (the polydisc $\Delta_\rho(a)$, polyradius, the bidisc, the unit polydisc) and the balls $B_\rho(a)$, $\mathbb B^n$
Definition 1.1.2 (holomorphic means locally bounded and separately complex differentiable) and the alternative $C^1$ Cauchy–Riemann definition
the Wirtinger operators $\partial/\partial z_k$ and $\partial/\partial\bar z_k$ in $n$ variables

Proposition 1.1.3 (a holomorphic function is infinitely differentiable and each $\partial f/\partial z_k$ is holomorphic), proved by iterating the one-variable Cauchy formula and differentiating under the integral
Theorem 1.1.4 (the Cauchy integral formula on a polydisc) and the distinguished boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Delta_1\times\cdots\times\partial\Delta_n$
Exercise 1.1.3 (the modulus of a function continuous on the closed polydisc and holomorphic inside attains its maximum on the distinguished boundary)
Exercise 1.1.5 (in the real setting separate differentiability does not give continuity, witnessed by $xy/(x^2+y^2)$)
Exercise 1.1.6 (holomorphy is equivalent to local boundedness together with holomorphy along every complex line)
Exercise 1.1.7 (a several-variable Morera theorem: continuity plus vanishing integrals over triangles lying in complex lines characterises holomorphy)
contents.reason: A characterisation by triangle integrals in complex lines, needing an oriented notion of a triangle inside $\mathbb C^n$ and its boundary. Nothing on this page verifies holomorphy from triangle integrals: every holomorphy proof here goes through the Cauchy formula or the power series, so the criterion would be built and never used.

contents.name: Exercise 1.1.8 (a continuous function on $\overline{\mathbb D^2}$, holomorphic off the origin, is bounded and extends holomorphically)
contents.reason: This is the punctured-bidisc case of the Riemann extension theorem, whose general form is Theorem 1.6.1 of the same source and also declined here; both belong with the removal of thin singular sets rather than with the foundations.

contents.name: §1.2 multi-index notation $z^\alpha$, $|z|^\alpha$, $\partial^{|\alpha|}/\partial z^\alpha$, $|\alpha|$, $\alpha!$
Theorem 1.2.1 (a continuous function holomorphic on a polydisc equals a power series converging uniformly absolutely on compact subsets, and conversely)
the converse half of Theorem 1.2.1 (a uniformly absolutely convergent power series defines a holomorphic function)

Proposition 1.2.2 (the derivative formula $\partial^{|\alpha|}f/\partial z^\alpha(z)$ as an integral over the distinguished boundary, the identification $c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$, and the Cauchy estimates)
the coefficient identification $c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ and its uniqueness consequence
Proposition 1.2.3 (a compactly uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, with all derivatives converging compactly uniformly)
Examples 1.2.4 and 1.2.5 and Proposition 1.2.6 (the domain of convergence of a power series is a complete Reinhardt domain, and the domain of convergence may have empty interior)
contents.reason: Domains of convergence are the entry point to Reinhardt geometry and logarithmic convexity, which is the subject the next pages of this track are for. This page needs convergence on polydiscs only, and every expansion it proves is anchored at a polydisc.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2.7 (identity theorem: vanishing on a nonempty open subset of a domain forces vanishing everywhere), with the clopen-set proof over all derivatives
Theorem 1.2.8 (maximum principle: a local maximum of $|f|$ on a domain forces $f$ to be constant)
Exercise 1.2.13 (Liouville in several variables from the one-variable theorem along complex lines)
Definition 1.2.9 (the ring $\mathcal O(U)$ of holomorphic functions) and Exercise 1.2.19 (it is an integral domain exactly when $U$ is connected)
Exercise 1.2.21 (zeros are never isolated in $\mathbb C^n$ for $n\ge2$)
Exercises 1.2.15 and 1.2.16 (the several-variable Montel and Hurwitz theorems)
contents.reason: Montel needs equicontinuity and a diagonal extraction, and Hurwitz in several variables needs a substitute for the one-variable zero-counting integral because zeros are not isolated. Neither is used by any item here, and the first belongs with normal families.

contents.name: Exercise 1.2.12 (a several-variable Schwarz lemma)
contents.reason: The Schwarz lemma is a one-variable result this library has not reached at this point in the reading order, so its several-variable analogue has no base case to rest on here.

contents.name: §1.3 Derivatives, Proposition 1.3.1 (the complex chain rule in Wirtinger form)
Definition 1.3.4 (a mapping into $\mathbb C^m$ is holomorphic when each component is) and Theorem 1.3.5 (composites of holomorphic mappings are holomorphic)
Proposition 1.3.6 (the chain rule $D(g\circ f)(p)=Dg(f(p))Df(p)$ for holomorphic mappings) and the holomorphic Jacobian matrix
Proposition 1.3.7 ($|\det Df(p)|^2=\det D_{\mathbb R}f(p)$, relating the holomorphic and real Jacobian determinants)
contents.reason: The identity compares the complex Jacobian with the real Jacobian of the underlying map of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, and its proof is a determinant computation on the block form of the realification. No item on this page needs the real determinant; the multiplicativity that the chain rule does need is recorded instead.

contents.name: Theorem 1.3.8 (the holomorphic implicit function theorem) and Exercise 1.3.6 (the holomorphic inverse function theorem)
contents.reason: Both are exactly the place where the target dimension matters, and the design for this track puts them on the page whose subject they are, together with the rank theorem and Weierstrass preparation. Their proofs also need the real implicit function theorem applied to the realification, machinery this page does not otherwise touch.

contents.name: §1.4 Inequivalence of ball and polydisc: Definition 1.4.1 (biholomorphic), Theorem 1.4.2 (the one-variable Riemann mapping theorem), Definition 1.4.3 (proper maps), Theorem 1.4.4 (Rothstein: no proper holomorphic map of the bidisc onto the ball), Definition 1.4.5 and Proposition 1.4.6 (analytic discs, and the sphere contains none), Lemma 1.4.7, Theorem 1.4.8
contents.reason: The whole section is the Poincaré non-equivalence and its proper-mapping strengthening. The design for this track fixes its home on the Bergman-kernel page, where an invariant supplies a proof; the argument here needs proper maps and boundary limits, neither of which this page develops.

contents.name: §1.5 Cartan’s uniqueness theorem (Theorem 1.5.1) and Corollary 1.5.2 (biholomorphisms of circular domains fixing the origin are linear)
contents.reason: Cartan’s theorem is proved by iterating the map and reading the vector-valued Cauchy estimates off the iterates on a bounded domain. It is a rigidity theorem about automorphisms, not part of the foundational equivalence this page establishes, and nothing here consumes it.

contents.name: §1.6 Theorem 1.6.1 (Riemann extension theorem across the zero set of a holomorphic $g$)
contents.reason: The removal of a thin singular set is the local content of the Hartogs phenomena, and its proof needs the one-variable Riemann extension theorem applied on slices together with control of the zero set. This page establishes no structure of zero sets.

contents.name: §1.6 Theorem 1.6.2 (the zero set of a nonzero holomorphic function has a dense open set of regular points on which it is a complex submanifold) and Theorem 1.6.6 (an injective holomorphic map $\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ has nonvanishing Jacobian)
contents.reason: Both rest on the local structure of zero sets, which in this library will come from Weierstrass preparation; the design for this track says so explicitly and places the isolated-zero statement there.

sources.title: H. P. Boas, Lecture Notes on Multidimensional Complex Analysis (Texas A&M, Math 650)
sources.locator: Ch. 1 §§1.1–1.5 (PDF pp. 3–7) and Ch. 2 §§2.1–2.7 (PDF pp. 9–38), read in full; Ch. 3 onward is outside the claimed range

contents.name: §1.1 A note on terminology (what "several" means in "several complex variables")
contents.reason: An essay on the English and German words for indefinite plurality. It contains no mathematical statement to scaffold, and the library fixes $m\ge1$ and says so.

contents.name: §1.2 Power series (the domain of absolute convergence of a multivariable power series, and Exercise 1)
§1.3 Integral representations (the iterated Cauchy integral on the bidisc and the distinguished boundary)
§1.4 Partial differential equations (the inhomogeneous Cauchy–Riemann system $\partial u/\partial\bar z_j=f_j$ and its compatibility condition)
contents.reason: The overdetermined $\bar\partial$ system and its solvability are a whole later development; this page states the homogeneous system only, as the characterisation of holomorphy for $C^1$ functions, and proves nothing about solving the inhomogeneous one.

contents.name: §1.5 Geometry (biholomorphic inequivalence of the ball and the bidisc, and Fatou–Bieberbach domains)
contents.reason: Both are geometric phenomena about the shape of domains rather than about the local theory of holomorphic functions, and the design for this track puts the non-equivalence where an invariant proves it.

contents.name: §2.1 Domain of convergence and §2.2 Characterization of domains of convergence, Theorem 1 (a complete Reinhardt domain is a domain of convergence iff it is logarithmically convex)
contents.reason: Logarithmic convexity of Reinhardt domains is the first genuine step into the geometry of holomorphy, and this page needs no more than convergence on a polydisc, which it proves directly from the kernel expansion.

contents.name: §2.3 Local properties of holomorphic functions: the iterated Cauchy formula, the geometric-series expansion of the kernel, uniqueness of $c_\alpha$, and $c_\alpha=f^{(\alpha)}(\zeta)/\alpha!$
the multivariable Cauchy estimates $|f^{(\alpha)}(\text{centre})|\le\alpha!\,M/r^\alpha$
the statement that holomorphic functions are infinitely differentiable, satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations in each variable, and obey a local maximum principle
the identity principle in the form valid in all dimensions, with the explicit warning that an accumulation point of zeros is not enough because zeros are never isolated
the normal-limit statement (a compactly uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, checked on small polydiscs)
Exercise 7 (a multidimensional Hurwitz theorem: a normal limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is zero-free or identically zero)
contents.reason: Boas points out that the one-variable zero-counting integral has no obvious analogue because zeros are not isolated, so a special argument is needed. That argument is not available from anything this page proves.

contents.name: §2.4 The Hartogs phenomenon, Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 (holomorphic extension from a Hartogs figure and from a spherical shell to the ball)
contents.reason: The extension phenomena are the subject of the next page of this track and depend on Laurent expansions in one variable applied on slices; this page proves nothing about extension.

contents.name: §2.5 Natural boundaries: Theorem 4 (Cartan–Thullen), Lemma 1 (Pringsheim’s lemma in arbitrary dimension), Theorem 5 (Paley–Zygmund), Lemma 2 (a Rademacher-series lemma)
contents.reason: These identify domains of convergence with domains of holomorphy and construct power series with natural boundaries, using probabilistic estimates on Rademacher functions. The tools are measure-theoretic and the subject is the geometry of holomorphy.

contents.name: §2.6 Summary: domains of convergence (logarithmic convexity, domain of convergence and domain of holomorphy coincide for complete Reinhardt domains)
contents.reason: A summary of the declined §§2.1, 2.2 and 2.5, so it declines with them; no separate statement of it is scaffolded here.

contents.name: §2.7 Theorem 6 (Hartogs: separate holomorphicity alone implies joint holomorphicity) and Lemma 3
contents.reason: This is exactly the theorem whose local-boundedness hypothesis this page keeps, and the design for this track states plainly that it is not folded into the foundations and is not cited in any proof here. Its own proof uses the subharmonicity of $\limsup$ of a normalised sequence.

contents.name: Theorem 7 (Osgood: separately holomorphic and locally bounded implies jointly holomorphic), with Method 1 by holomorphy of the coefficient functions and Method 2 by the Schwarz-lemma continuity estimate
the observation that a continuous separately holomorphic function is representable by the iterated Cauchy integral
Theorem 8 (Osgood: a separately holomorphic function is jointly holomorphic on a dense open subset), proved with the Baire category theorem
contents.reason: A partial result superseded by Hartogs’s theorem, which this track places on the next page; building it here would mean building the weaker statement on the page that deliberately keeps the boundedness hypothesis, with no consumer.

contents.name: Exercise 14 (a separately polynomial function on $\mathbb C^2$ is jointly polynomial)
contents.reason: A separate-to-joint statement about polynomials rather than about holomorphic functions, needing a degree bound argument this page has no reason to develop.

sources.title: M. Jabbari, Notes for Analysis and Geometry of Several Complex Variables (CIMAT)
sources.locator: Ch. 3 opening and §3.1 (PDF pp. 26–28) and §3.3 with Remark 40 (PDF pp. 44–46), read in full; §3.2 and §§3.4 onward are outside the claimed range

contents.name: Theorem 22(1) (the Cauchy integral formula for polydiscs, obtained by applying the one-variable formula $m$ times on a slightly smaller polydisc)
Theorem 22(2) (holomorphic functions are smooth and their complex derivatives are holomorphic)
Theorem 22(3) (Bergman’s estimate: $\lVert\partial^\alpha f\rVert_K\le C_\alpha\lVert f\rVert_{L^1(D’)}$)
contents.reason: The estimate bounds derivatives by an $L^1$ norm over a neighbourhood, which needs Lebesgue integration on $\mathbb C^m$ and the polar decomposition of the volume element. The supremum-norm Cauchy estimate that this page does need is proved instead.

contents.name: Theorem 22(4) (Weierstrass: compactly uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic, with convergence of every complex derivative)
Theorem 22(5) (Montel: a locally equibounded sequence has a compactly uniformly convergent subsequence)
contents.reason: Montel needs the Arzelà–Ascoli extraction, which this library develops for function spaces but which no item on this page consumes; the design for this track places normal families on their own page.

contents.name: Theorem 22(6) (unique normal power series representation on a polydisc, the coefficient integral, and $|a_\alpha|\le r^{-\alpha}\sup|f|$)
the geometric-series identity $\prod_j(\zeta_j-z_j)^{-1}=\sum_\alpha z^\alpha\prod_j\zeta_j^{-\alpha_j-1}$ used in the proof of Theorem 22(6)
Theorem 22(7) (identity theorem, in both the matching-derivatives form and the nonempty-open-subset form)
Theorem 22(8) (maximum modulus principle, interior and up-to-boundary forms)
Theorem 22(9) (open mapping theorem), proved by restricting to the complex line through a point where $f$ does not vanish
the exercise that $|f(z)|\le C|z|_2^k$ on $\mathbb C^m$ forces $f$ to be a polynomial of total degree at most $k$
contents.reason: A growth-rigidity statement whose proof needs the Cauchy estimates on balls of growing radius together with a degree count over multi-indices. It is a genuine consequence but no item here uses it, and its one-variable ancestor already sits published on the analyticity page.

contents.name: the exercise giving the unique normal Laurent representation on a closed polyannulus, with vanishing of the negative coefficients when an inner radius is zero
contents.reason: Laurent expansion in several variables is the tool the Hartogs extension theorem runs on, and the design for this track puts it there; this page develops the Maclaurin theory only.

contents.name: the exercise that a normal limit of nowhere-zero holomorphic functions is nowhere zero or identically zero
contents.reason: The several-variable Hurwitz statement, declined here for the same reason Boas gives: the one-variable proof counts zeros with an integral, and zeros are not isolated in dimension at least two.

contents.name: the exercise giving the several-variable Schwarz lemma on the polydisc and on the ball
contents.reason: It rests on the one-variable Schwarz lemma, which this library has not reached at this point in the reading order.

contents.name: §3.3 Remark 40 (the equivalence of the power-series definition, the $C^1$ Cauchy–Riemann definition, and separate holomorphy, and which implications need Hartogs)
§3.3 Theorem 38 (a subset of $\mathbb C^m$ is a domain of convergence iff it is a logarithmically convex complete Reinhardt domain) and Lemma 39 (Abel’s lemma)
